#1431. Some are calling this 'Tuchel 2.0' and his latest squad does feel like that. Here's why England think a tilt at the European Championship is within reach, writes IAN LADYMAN

Published: 17:35 EST, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 05:45 EST, 9 November 2026

One of Thomas Tuchel’s favourite analogies when it comes to the development of his England team is that of a train leaving a station with only the chosen few on it. As time moves on, the bodies lying on the tracks are growing greater in number.

Consider this statistic. Of the 26 players who travelled to the World Cup in America 13 are not in the squad chosen by England manager Tuchel for next week’s Nations League games against Croatia and Spain. And that does not include Cole Palmer and Phil Foden who, after missing out in the summer, were expected by many of us to have forced a way back in by now.

Tuchel’s latest selection has been affected by injuries, of course. But more significant is that the experienced German believes he is now starting to see an England team and squad develop in a way and in a direction that even he hadn’t envisaged once Argentina ended his World Cup hopes in that dismal Atlanta semi-final in July.

Different feelings, different style of play and, to a degree, different players.

Some are calling this ‘Tuchel 2.0’ and it does feel a little bit like that. The start of the second phase of Tuchel’s tenure, the start of the road towards a tilt at another trophy, the European Championships of 2028.

Having admitted to some worry ahead of the four-game international break FIFA saddled us all with last month, Tuchel sat down yesterday looking and sounding like a man once again certain of himself.

Tuchel sat down with the media looking and sounding like a man once again certain of himself

The inclusion of Jobe Bellingham — Jude’s younger brother (right) — was the headline act but there were other messages written within

Certain enough of a direct, quick, athletic style of play that helped England to two wins over Czech Republic and one – by seven goals – against Croatia in Rijeka. And certain that a dependence on players like Jordan Henderson, Dan Burn and John Stones for what we may politely call ‘squad culture management’ lies now in the past.

All of this may crash down in Madrid next Sunday. Spain have already beaten Tuchel’s England once – at Wembley in late September – and a repeat this month would ask familiar questions about England against the really good teams.

But for now, Tuchel is confident enough to claim that he has found his path.

‘We said at some point we need to take the next step, to build on what we have, to get better and to improve otherwise you’re just left behind,’ said Tuchel yesterday.

‘That’s how football works. You have been champion in one season but you need to improve, you need to bring in new players for competition, young players, new energy, fresh energy. It’s also the way, naturally, the national team goes.

‘We cannot be stuck in the same personnel and in the same style of play.

‘I agreed with you last month. I was the first to admit I was not 100 per cent happy with the pure level of football we played in the US. I saw a higher level in training [than on the field], I saw a higher level in glimpses.

‘We adjusted some things tactically, created some new positions and took the next steps.’

The Tuchel we sat down with in late September still wore the scars of the summer’s disappointment – and the criticism that came with it – rather visibly. It was the first time we had seen him like that in his two years in the job. He was tetchy and easily provoked. Call it the Argentina effect if you like.

Here, he appeared rather healed. Good results tend to do that for a manager and a little time helps too. If he believes his team has moved on then maybe he has also and he had to.

Certainly, his selection squad speaks to that. The inclusion of Jobe Bellingham – Jude’s younger brother – was the headline act but there were other messages written within.

Henderson and Burn are available but not included. So too Arsenal’s Noni Madueke, excluded to the benefit of the more direct Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha.

‘We need runners who will go between the lines,’ said Tuchel. A clear indication, there, that too much of England’s summer wing play was too slow and too conservatively narrow.

Palmer, Foden and Kobbie Mainoo are also on the outside looking in once again and the case of the Manchester United midfielder is perhaps indicative of how Tuchel now operates.

Moved to apologise to him in front of the whole squad in July for his lack of minutes at the World Cup, Tuchel was determined Mainoo would play in the opening four games of the Nations League campaign.

‘I was desperate to give him the minutes and desperate to include him in this new start,’ explained Tuchel.

‘But then he pulled out. He missed an excellent camp and also entered a difficult, difficult spell for himself.

‘Man United fell off a cliff a little bit performance-wise. So this is why he now suffers.’

We can talk about the whys and wherefores of that logic. If Mainoo was good enough in September then why is he not good enough now? How desperate could Tuchel really have been to play him that one withdrawal with injury closed the door for the next camp and opened it instead for Bellingham jnr?

This, though, is how Tuchel works. He is an adept tactician but he’s also a mood coach, someone who – after sobering club experiences at places like PSG, Chelsea and Bayern Munich – places huge emphasis on environments and gut feels and culture. If he feels something works, he doesn’t like to pick it apart without good reason.

This is why for example the growing voice and influence of Elliot Anderson has left Jordan Henderson suddenly surplus. Tuchel says the door is not closed on a player who will be 38 by the time the next Euros are played and he called him this week to say so. In Tuchel’s mind, though, England will now move without the veteran and others of his ilk.

‘I was concerned before the last camp that we missed the players who kept our standards,’ said Tuchel.

‘I was worried that we missed so many of them. But then this group found their own way and their own voices.

It’s also reasonable to ask why our head coach can’t find room in his squad – if not his team – for the game changing duo of Palmer and Foden

‘I know what the others did. They built a platform on which these ones can build.’

Time will tell. To a degree, Spain will tell. Can England play the kind of higher tempo, front foot football we saw against Croatia and the Czechs against the world and European champions next Sunday? They embarrassed us when we didn’t have the ball at Wembley.

It’s also reasonable to ask why our head coach can’t find room in his squad – if not his team – for the game-changing duo of Palmer and Foden. England lacked good substitutes at the World Cup. There was too much like for like.

England need to win in order for such decisions to be vindicated and Tuchel knows that.

Asked yesterday if he felt as invigorated as he looked he said he did. ‘The last camp gave me a lot of energy, gave me a lot of extra belief,’ he said.

‘It gave me a lot of optimism to not compromise on the way England teams should play. Be physical but also step up in the pure level of performances.’

It’s certainly time for this now. The summer only served to expose English shortcomings. Tuchel’s train must arrive in Madrid next weekend, not only with fresh personnel but also new ideas clearly apparent.

#1430. Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” said Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

He told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a big difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”

The veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

#1429. Mysterious anthrax outbreak kills hippos in Africa — raising concerns for human spread

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

Hippos in Virunga National Park in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have been affected by an anthrax outbreak over the past month.Credit: Evelyn Hockstein/MCT/Tribune News Service via Getty

An anthrax outbreak has killed at least 30 hippopotamuses in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in the past month. No cases in people have been reported so far, but authorities say they are monitoring the situation closely.

The dead animals were first found in September in Virunga National Park in eastern DRC, and laboratory tests confirmed they died from anthrax, a serious infectious disease caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis.

The outbreak comes at the same time as health authorities and conservation groups in the DRC manage large outbreaks of Ebola and cholera, and the ongoing humanitarian challenges caused by armed conflict in the region. A disease outbreak of anthrax in wildlife puts further pressure on already limited resources, say researchers.

The anthrax bacterium is found naturally in soil worldwide and can infect livestock and wild animals if they encounter its spores. Officials at Virunga National Park said in a statement that teams have been monitoring the affected area and coordinating the safe handling and disposal of carcasses and there have been no new deaths in the past two weeks.

David Hayman, a disease ecologist at Massey University in Palmerston North, New Zealand, says the main risk to people is from handling infected carcasses or consuming contaminated meat. The disease can be treated with antibiotics if caught early, but it can be fatal without treatment.

Although no cases have been reported in people during this outbreak, Charity Mutesi, an epidemiologist at the Uganda National Institute of Public Health in Kampala, says that infections can go undetected because people might decide to stay at home rather than going to a clinic for treatment. People often use herbs on the lesions caused by some anthrax infections, or might seek care from drug shops, private clinics or traditional healers, who do not report the cases to the national disease surveillance systems, she adds.

The DRC has experienced several anthrax outbreaks in animals and people over the past few years. In March 2025, an outbreak killed around 65 hippos. Fifteen people tested positive for the disease in bordering Uganda, two of whom died.

“It is very concerning that these outbreaks continue to happen,” says Ricardo Soares Magalhães, an epidemiologist at the University of Queensland in Brisbane, Australia.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03580-4

#1428. Inside Cristiano Ronaldo Jr's bid to step out of his father's shadow after his Portugal Under-17s call-up: From padel beef with Rio Ferdinand to a Coca-Cola BAN

Published: 02:00 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 05:50 EST, 9 November 2026

He has spent his whole life being measured against European football's greatest goalscorer. Now Cristiano Ronaldo Jr. has taken his biggest step yet.

The 16-year-old has been called up to Portugal's U17 squad for the first time, and will face Andorra on November 11 and Serbia on November 14. And the timing is hard to ignore.

The famous No. 7 shirt Ronaldo Sr wore for two decades will now be vacant after he announced his retirement from international football on Thursday.

It's a heavy shirt for anyone to inherit. Luis Figo graced the number when he led Portugal’s golden generation to the 2006 World Cup semi-finals, and Ronaldo Sr himself carried it when he captained them to the European Championship in 2016. Both won the Ballon d’Or and are two of the most tantalising players the nation has ever produced.

Portugal’s power vacuum is also a pressure point. As the son of the man who wore that shirt, Ronaldo Jr. will attract more attention, and more expectation.

The national team lacks its focal point, and few names carry more weight than his. He is the natural successor in marketing terms, if nothing else. Whether he is the player to take it is another matter.

Cristiano Ronaldo Jr - son of the Portuguese great - is looking to forge his own football career

This week the 16-year-old earned his first call-up to Portugal's U17 team

The weight of his father's expectations has been there from the start. Ronaldo Jr once floated the idea of becoming a goalkeeper, and his father’s reaction was swift. “No, I don’t want that! Are you joking or what?” Ronaldo Sr responds in the 2015 documentary Ronaldo.

Up front for the Juventus academy, his record would make the man chasing 1,000 career goals jealous: a staggering 58 goals in 23 games for the Under-9s. Yet his father was never satisfied. Asked at the 2020 Globe Soccer Awards, with his son sitting in the audience, whether the boy had what it takes to reach the top, Ronaldo Sr’s answer was blunt.

“Not yet,” he said. “I’m hard with him sometimes because he drinks Coca-Cola and Fanta. (He has) chips and fries; I fight with him.”

Hard data on his youth career since then is limited. Reports of his interest in switching to the Real Madrid academy suggested a desire to develop and compete.

Rio Ferdinand, who played alongside Ronaldo Sr. at Manchester United, has seen that competitive streak in the son on the padel court.

“I was in the Red Sea a couple of days ago; I play padel every day. (When) me and Cristiano Jr. get mad, we don't speak for like two days.” He exclaimed on Five Presents. Like his father, he doesn’t take losing well.

His body, though, has settled the question of position. At 6 ft 3 in, he already stands taller than his father. Growth spurts may temporarily cost him some of the pace and the effortless coordination of his youth. A forced adaption of his style is not unusual: Ronaldo’s former teammates Gareth Bale and Scott McTominay were both moved into new positions to begin their professional careers.

It is also a path his father walked. Forget stepovers, flicks and trademark ‘Ronaldo chop’. Jr’s game is currently closer to the Ronaldo of Juventus and the Old Trafford return: a penalty-box predator who lives on timing and movement rather than dribbling past defenders.

The young striker has represented the youth academies of Man United, Real Madrid and Juventus

But his ultra-professional father said his son needs to cut out the Coca-Cola if he wants to make it at the top level

His Portugal numbers are respectable, not remarkable. Five goals in 13 appearances is a decent return, but he has played just 522 minutes, an average of around 40 per game, and scored roughly once every 104 minutes. However, it is a tiny sample size.

To reach the top, he will need the work ethic his father is famous for. “I’ve never seen a more professional person,” Paul Scholes, Ronaldo Sr’s former Manchester United teammate, told Premier League Productions. “He was out there all day long, practising … he had weights on his ankles.”

Habits like that are built in demanding environments, and Jr’s has been a gentle one.

Playing in Saudi Arabia still has its positives. As Jr. transitions from boy to man, weaker opposition has given him room to grow into his body and build confidence as he prepares for men's senior football. But that breathing space has a shelf life.

He has options. He could stay and share a dressing room with his father, or return to one of the academies of Ronaldo Sr’s former clubs, with Real Madrid, Juventus and Manchester United all reported by The Sun to be interested. He has the name, the call-up and the options, but not yet the proof.

When Ronaldo Sr walked away from Portugal, he left behind a shirt, a record and a question. Saudi Arabia cannot give his son the answer. If he wants international caps and Champions League football, he must leave Al Nassr and his old man for a stage where nobody gives him an inch.

The surname opened the door. Only he can walk through it.

#1427. Fine-tuning brain stimulation to fight Parkinson’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Liam Drew is a freelance science journalist based near London.

Stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (orange) can lead to changes in multiple nerve tracts.Credit: Nanditha Rajamani

Sixteen years ago, Simon Little was a junior neurologist thinking of devoting his time to international health work. But then he attended a lecture by Peter Brown.

Brown, a neuroscientist at the University of Oxford, UK, described his studies of people with Parkinson’s disease who had had electrodes implanted in their brains. The electrodes were intended to treat symptoms of this neurodegenerative disease by targeting electrical pulses to structures deep inside the brain. But to start with, Brown used them to record the oscillating waves of neuronal electricity that these brain structures emitted.

The recordings showed that as a person’s symptoms ebbed and flowed — their movements slowing then normalizing, their tremors flaring and subsiding — the oscillations changed1. “I was completely fascinated,” Little says. “The music of the brain was encoding something really powerful about people’s symptoms.”

After the lecture, Little asked Brown if he could do a PhD with him. Little laughs as he recalls how Brown tried to warn him off, saying that the field was a complete backwater and that Little would be pursuing this work at his own professional risk.

Undeterred, Little joined Brown’s laboratory, and the risk paid off. Little, now at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), and Brown took the signal most strongly related to the intensity of Parkinson’s symptoms — an oscillation in what’s termed the beta band, occurring 12–30 times per second — and used it as the trigger for deep brain stimulation (DBS).

Typically, DBS zaps the brain constantly. But by activating the device only when beta activity crested, Little and Brown could provide stimulation when a person most needed it. In an initial trial, numerical ratings of volunteers’ mobility were about 30% better than they were with constant stimulation2. “We found that less was more,” Little says.

Last year, the first ‘closed loop’ or adaptive DBS (aDBS) system for Parkinson’s, which operates similarly to the set-up that Little and Brown used in their early experiments, was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and earned a CE mark to be sold in the European Union. The technology — made by Medtronic in Minneapolis, Minnesota — uses the same electrodes to record beta-band activity and stimulate the brain.

Although this system is clinically effective, researchers think that it provides only a fraction of what smart implanted neurotechnologies could one day offer people with Parkinson’s. “This is a breakthrough,” says Wolf-Julian Neumann, a neuroscientist at Charité University Medicine in Berlin. “But it’s a super-tiny step towards the vision that we are pursuing.”

Neumann, Little and others say that emerging techniques and hardware now being tested in small clinical trials will lead to devices that decode, on the basis of neural activity, what someone with Parkinson’s is doing — say, sleeping, walking or speaking — and the exact symptoms they are experiencing. Then, with this real-time information, devices will deliver different forms of electrical stimulation to alleviate users’ symptoms and aid their movements3. “It’s a totally different way of conceptualizing the treatment of brain disorders,” says Neumann.

Parkinson’s disease is characterized by degeneration of the brain’s substantia nigra, a cluster of neurons that produces the neurotransmitter dopamine. This dopamine regulates the brain networks that coordinate voluntary movements. Without it, that system malfunctions.

“In Parkinson’s disease, you’ve got an unwanted brain arrhythmia,” says Helen Bronte-Stewart, a neuroscientist at Stanford University in California. The extent to which neurons synchronize their firing at beta-band frequencies is abnormally high, producing a disruptive signal, she says. “It’s jamming the brain’s ability to coordinate movement.”

This leads to the hallmark symptoms of Parkinson’s: slowed movements, rigidity and tremors. The disease can also cause postural changes, speech difficulties and non-motor symptoms, such as depression or anxiety. In its later stages, cognitive decline is common. The standard treatment is to boost a person’s dopamine levels by dosing them with the drug levodopa. But levodopa can cause side effects, such as uncontrolled movements, and people can experience periods in which the drug’s effectiveness blinks on and off.

Since its clinical approval in 1997, DBS has emerged as a popular alternative for people whose Parkinson’s isn’t well controlled by drugs. Far and away the most common type of brain implant in use today, DBS has done much to normalize the process of undergoing neurosurgery to have a therapeutic device fitted. In its original form, the DBS electrodes — connected by wires that run down the recipient’s neck to a small power pack implanted in the chest — deliver a constant, high-frequency train of electrical pulses. Their target is either the subthalamic nucleus or the globus pallidus, two brain regions that are components of the movement network modulated by dopamine.

Simon Little (right) follows his patient Deb Zeyen as she demonstrates motor improvements.Credit: Yalonda M. James/Polaris/eyevine

Andreas Horn, a neuroscientist at the University of Cologne in Germany, says that ‘stimulation’ is a misnomer in DBS. The high-frequency zapping, he says, “is more about disrupting or overriding some circuitry that’s become dysfunctional”.

The change from continuous DBS to aDBS demanded that Medtronic incorporate the necessary technology into a compact medical device. Little says that in his first experiments, volunteers were wired up to racks of computers, filters and stimulators. Medtronic miniaturized that hardware so that it all fitted into the small implanted power pack.

Bronte-Stewart led the trial that secured the device’s approval4. This showed that aDBS was safe and that it controlled recipients’ symptoms effectively. The trial — somewhat controversially, Bronte-Stewart acknowledges — didn’t directly compare aDBS with conventional, continuous DBS. But just sending people on aDBS home and trusting they’d be safe was a groundbreaking step, she says.

Since 2020, Medtronic has been supplying a system capable of running either continuous or aDBS, and roughly 25,000 recipients could potentially switch to aDBS now. However, scientists are already taking note of the limitations of this system — and of using beta-band oscillations as a trigger.

One issue is that current aDBS systems take weeks of inpatient programming, with neurologists observing the effects of different sets of manually selected stimulation parameters5. “For this to scale, you can’t have every Parkinson’s patient needing three weeks of a neurologist monitoring them and optimizing this,” says Doris Wang, a neurosurgeon at UCSF.

Another issue is that beta oscillations provide only a crude indication of overall symptoms. “Beta power is essentially a biomarker of global worsening of symptoms of Parkinson’s disease,” says Neumann. Although this information is no doubt useful — not least, says Neumann, for effectively up- and downregulating DBS as levodopa’s effects change — beta-band oscillations don’t discern exactly what someone is experiencing. “Tremor actually reduces beta,” he says. As a result, “the beta-based adaptive DBS algorithm can confuse tremor for a good symptom state.”

What’s more, in current systems that use the same electrodes to stimulate the brain and record activity, artefacts from the stimulation compromise the quality of recorded signals6. Plus, these systems are recording from sites in the brain that are selected because they are best places to stimulate, and not necessarily the most informative to record from.

To address these issues and offer much finer control of the disease’s various manifestations, researchers are seeking to develop next-generation aDBS systems. On the input side, they are harnessing advances in brain–computer interfaces, including fresh technologies for recording and decoding brain activity. These, the researchers say, will be able to decipher exactly what users are doing and what symptoms are occurring.

On the output side, clinical studies are showing that it’s possible to halt symptoms of Parkinson’s by targeting separate neural pathways. For instance, Horn’s group has found that, by targeting adjacent but distinct nerve-fibre tracts (using conventional continuous stimulation), they can selectively help with tremor, rigidity, slow movement, or postural and gait-related problems7. “This is not so much about when to stimulate,” Horn says, “but rather about where and what to simulate.”

To map which nerve-fibre tracts passed close to the DBS electrodes, Horn’s team took brain scans of people who had had Medtronic devices implanted in the subthalamic nucleus. The scans showed tracts originating from different parts of the brain, such as the motor cortex or cerebellum, running near to the four contact sites on each electrode.

The researchers then stimulated various combinations of contact sites to steer currents to different chosen tracts. To their surprise, targeting specific fibre tracts ameliorated symptoms individually.

Horn and colleagues then developed an algorithm that, given a set of symptoms, will choose stimulation sites that should provide the most benefit. “If a patient has a lot of tremor, we tell the algorithm, ‘find me the stimulation volume that will maximally engage the tremor tract and not so much the other tracts’,” says Nanditha Rajamani, a neuroscientist at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts, who collaborated with Horn on this project.

In a small, five-person trial, the algorithm’s suggested settings produced a bigger improvement in the symptoms of four participants than did the stimulation their neurologists had previously set up for them7. The fifth person’s symptoms neither improved nor worsened.

Looking ahead, Horn says that because the manifestations of Parkinson’s shift constantly, the ability to target each symptom type could enable adaptive devices that suppress only the symptoms a person is currently dealing with. But that will require the device to ‘know’ what those symptoms are, meaning that researchers must identify the neural correlates of each symptom type.

To do so, they are recording brain activity while volunteers use wearable devices, such as accelerometers, to precisely track arm and leg movements. Increasingly, recordings are acquired not just from DBS electrodes deep in the brain, but also from a separate set of electrodes placed on the brain surface. These cortical electrodes pick up the signals that arise in the motor cortex to initiate and control movements. “There is a lot more information in the cerebral cortex,” Wang says.

Neumann’s group, for example, has used machine learning to link hundreds of features captured in such neural recordings to both symptoms and drug side effects. The features the researchers used correlated with symptoms better than beta activity did. And importantly, the model worked in people whose data had not been used to develop it.

Neumann thinks that this approach might even allow researchers to identify neural signals that precede symptoms. If so, future systems might not just react to symptoms as they occur, but could also pre-emptively stimulate the brain to prevent tremors and other typical manifestations of Parkinson’s from occurring at all. “When you and I intend to move, there’s a huge spike of dopamine release,” he notes. A well-timed burst of electrical stimulation could functionally substitute for this in people with Parkinson’s and thereby ease upcoming movements.

Neuroscientist Helen Bronte-Stewart assesses someone with Parkinson’s disease.Credit: Yalonda M. James/Polaris/eyevine

Neumann also thinks that if a smart DBS system can decode what a person is doing, or trying to do, this could help to select the stimulation activity that best serves that person. For instance, he says, the high-intensity stimulation that suppresses tremor can make it difficult to speak, so if brain signals indicate that a person is attempting to talk, then the tremor-suppressing stimulation might be turned down, or even off.

Likewise, Bronte-Stewart, Little and Wang are searching for neural correlates of movements and symptoms, with a view to controlling stimulation8. Little and Bronte-Stewart are also keen to treat symptoms of Parkinson’s that are not related to movement by finding appropriate signals and target structures to combat mood symptoms and cognitive difficulties, respectively9.

In June, Wang published a small trial that began to put the pieces together. It used movement-related brain signals to address a hugely problematic aspect of Parkinson’s: gait freezing, in which people who are walking suddenly become unable to move and so fall10.

After identifying cortical and subcortical signals that indicated the motions of walking, Wang’s group used them to trigger brief stimulation on the relevant side of the brain — the right side to affect the movement of the left leg, and vice versa. People who received this intervention fell less frequently than those who did not. “It’s the first demonstration that such rapid, movement-specific aDBS or closed-loop DBS is possible,” Wang says. Trial participants said that movement felt smoother and more fluid when using the system, and that it was easier for them to get up and walk.

It’s safe to say that Brown was wrong when he told Little that attempting to relate brain signals to disease symptoms was a dead end. But over the years, what it takes to bridge the gulf between exploratory research and a clinical product has become more apparent. “Our role as researchers is to show what’s possible,” Little says. Only then can the different questions regarding what can be scaled up into a viable clinical intervention begin to be addressed.

Already, there are questions about next-generation DBS that did not apply to the first adaptive systems. For instance, Little notes that if extra cortical recording electrodes are needed, surgeons will need to learn a new implantation procedure.

He is also wary of emerging systems being heavily dependent on artificial intelligence — either to decode brain activity or to get systems up and running without weeks of manual programming. Concerns swirl about embedding uninterpretable AI technology in medical devices, especially when people’s welfare and behaviour depend on it.

Little questions what would happen if someone using an AI-powered DBS system experienced a major mishap, such as freezing completely or crashing their car, because the algorithm changed its stimulation patterns. “Who bears responsibility for that?” Little says. This is an evolving space for both developers and regulators, who must find a sweet spot with which all parties are comfortable, he says.

The transformation of an idea into a clinical product is a balancing act between what’s possible and what’s plausible, reliable and safe. As Parkinson’s researchers aim to again lead the way in new forms of neurotechnology, they will need to navigate the known and unknown challenges that arise. As Bronte-Stewart says, today’s advances “are coming out of really good labs in academic centres doing a lot of computational work. How is that going to filter down into something that can be embedded in a system in your chest?”

#1426. Forest Green apologise for failing to commemorate Remembrance Day at a home match due to 'mistake'

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 10:15 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 07:03 EST, 9 November 2026

Forest Green Rovers have apologised for failing to commemorate Remembrance Day at a home game, labelling it as 'human error' and a 'mistake' from the club.

Remembrance Day is November 11 with Forest Green's sole fixture around that date having been Saturday's 2-0 FA Cup first-round defeat at Luton Town. Both teams commemorated the occasion ahead of kick-off at Kenilworth Road.

Forest Green's last home fixture prior to that was a 2-2 draw with Harrogate Town on October 31 in the National League.

That encounter at The New Lawn saw supporters of the fifth-tier side take to a fan forum post-match questioning why nothing was in place for Remembrance Day - due to their then-forthcoming clash with Luton being an away tie.

Forest Green CEO Dane Vince replied on the club's Fan Advisory Board, admitting it was an oversight on their part.

'The lack of Remembrance at a home game is simply down to a human error/mistake on the club,' he wrote.

Forest Green Rovers have apologised for not commemorating Remembrance Day at a home game (National League side pictured doing so during Saturday's FA Cup 2-0 defeat at Luton)

Forest Green failed to do so in their home draw vs Harrogate on October 31, calling it a 'mistake'

Vince continued that a condensed schedule in this period didn't help matters, but still acknowledged that the club should have done more.

'It didn't help that we had a sizable number of games in a small time frame (including the FA Cup replay) beforehand; albeit that isn't an excuse, we should have got this right.'

Following the incident, Vince confirmed that Forest Green would contact the Royal British Legion for advice on future commemorations to ensure this wouldn't happen again. He also underlined that the missed home commemoration did not signal any change in the club's support for Remembrance or the Royal British Legion.

'This was a simple error/mistake,' he reiterated.

#1425. Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

Neto fires past Pickford to double Chelsea's lead! 🔥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SOJeBP5mq0

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

Already booked, Rogers was fortunate not to receive a second caution for a lunge on James Garner which took the man after the ball. A replica challenge by Everton’s Harrison Armstrong had warranted a yellow card in Tierney’s world just 21 minutes earlier.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

That should not disguise how this is a different Chelsea, contrasting not just with the characterless and rudderless team of last season, but also the defensively flawed version that began this one. Mike Penders deputised for the stricken Martínez – conscious but taken to hospital as a precaution – and was well-protected.

As much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

He signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Alonso’s anticipation of a fixture in which a battle had to be fought before there was an outbreak of football proved correct, aided by the fussy and generally terrible first-half officiating of Tierney.

Bizarrely, Alonso had as much cause to curse Tierney for the first of several contentious decisions, booking Armstrong for an aggressive but ultimately fair lunging challenge on Josh Acheampong. That enraged the home supporters to inspire Everton to their most dangerous spell, Thierno Barry coming closest to troubling Martínez before half-time.

Although Moisés Caicedo was denied a goal-of-the-season contender when a vicious 20-yard volley struck the crossbar, the scrappy, stop-start flavour of the occasion initially suited the hosts.

“They didn’t score, but did a fantastic job for the team,” Alonso pointedly said of his attackers.

Alonso’s name has not echoed so loudly across the Mersey since he played a few miles down the road from Everton’s new home. After several calamitous appointments, those fans can believe their team are in safe hands again.

A good win for Chelsea at Everton, but above all, let’s hope Martinez is back to full health soon.

Moyes accepted that his side had were not good enough.

He told TNT Sports: “We were a little bit unlucky with the goals. It wasn’t good defending, but it takes a couple of deflections before it gets to Neto. It makes it a relatively easy finish for him.

“The second one was a free-kick which obviously ricochets around, so I think there were parts of the game we did OK, but we didn’t offer enough to create enough, to make enough chances. I can’t think of many, so that is probably the biggest indictment.”

He had a minor gripe over a first-half tackle that was reviewed, saying, “I think the Morgan Rogers tackle on Jimmy [Garner] could have been questioned.”

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

#1424. Crisis-hit FIFA chief Gianni Infantino 'requested VIP treatment for his daughters and their dogs at Miami airport'

By DANIEL MATTHEWS, US SENIOR SPORTS WRITER

Published: 09:47 EST, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 12:07 EST, 9 November 2026

FIFA president Gianni Infantino is facing more uncomfortable questions after it emerged that his office asked for 'VIP treatment' for his daughters and their pet dogs on a trip from Miami to Qatar.

Infantino's future has been under the microscope after a scandal-laden few months, with honorary Japanese FA president Kohzo Tashima announcing on Thursday that he will stand against Infantino in next year's presidential election.

On Thursday, The Times revealed that back in May, Infantino's presidential office wrote to Miami airport officials asking for someone to 'assist' three of his daughters - and their pets - through security for a personal trip to Qatar.

Miami airport's VIP protocol reportedly allows diplomats and other special guests to be escorted through security checkpoints up to the door of the plane. Officers can also request early boarding.

These privileges are not automatically laid on for loved ones traveling separately, with protocol stating that 'courtesies... will not be extended' to family members of VIPs 'when the families are traveling on their own.'

But according to documents reviewed by the Daily Mail, members of Infantino's family enjoyed the airport's services dozens of times while traveling without the FIFA president between 2024 and 2026.

Gianni Infantino's office reportedly requested 'VIP treatment' for his daughters and their dogs

The FIFA president's future has been under the microscope after a scandal-laden few months

In a statement to The Times, Miami airport insisted these requests are dealt with 'on a case-by-case basis.' The Daily Mail has contacted FIFA for comment but a spokesperson told The Times: 'Port courtesy requests were made to Miami international airport (MIA), on the advice of a former adviser to the Fifa president.

'Port courtesies are provided at no charge to the president of Fifa given his position as the head of an association or NGO. Mr Infantino’s family members are also entitled to request these services under MIA’s own Courtesies of Port Handbook and these are also provided free of any charge, on a case-by-case basis, at the discretion of MIA.'

Infantino's position is already under threat heading into FIFA's presidential election next March, when he is hoping to be elected to a fourth term. Back in December, Infantino awarded Trump the inaugural FIFA Peace Prize – to widespread ridicule.

During the World Cup, the Balogun affair saw Infantino accused of favoritism and caving to the White House, while the FIFA president and Trump were mocked for handing over the trophy to Spain together.

Before long, Infantino faced a mutiny over his secret plans – later scrapped – to sell a stake in the World Cup to private equity investors including Joshua Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Then earlier this week, FIFA strongly denied allegations that Infantino influenced Trump administration officials to fast-track a work permit for his undocumented Nicaraguan housekeeper after she lost her legal status, according to bombshell documents.

The global soccer chief is alleged to have turned to politically-connected contacts to secure a new work permit for Yajarlin del Socorro Fernandez after the White House revoked her legal permission to work in the United States, according to documents reviewed by the Daily Mail.

Ana Maria Jaramillo is in the Complexity Science Hub, 1030 Vienna, Austria, and Graz Technical University, Graz, Austria.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are designed to isolate cause and effect. They have become important instruments for evaluating interventions in medicine, economics and public health. Their strength comes from assigning ‘treatments’ independently of the characteristics of the participants. However, people live in communities, and interventions delivered to individuals can have consequences far beyond the outcome that researchers set out to measure. Writing in Nature, Papamichalis et al.1 highlight this phenomenon.

#1422. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

9 - Florian Wirtz's nine chances created from open play against Brentford is the most by a player in a Premier League game since Sadio Mané v Burnley in January 2021 (9) and the most by a player in an away game since Samir Nasri v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Progress. https://t.co/xyMIQP9y5p

Liverpool break and their sweeping move up the field comes to Wirtz whose cut-back picks out Szoboszlai perfectly but the midfielder miscues and his effort does not trouble Kelleher.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1421. Embattled FIFA chief Gianni Infantino 'used Trump adviser to get work permit for his undocumented Nicaraguan housekeeper'

By ISABEL BALDWIN, US ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 15:01 EST, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 12:08 EST, 9 November 2026

FIFA President Gianni Infantino allegedly influenced Trump administration officials to fast-track a work permit for his undocumented Nicaraguan housekeeper after she lost her legal status, according to bombshell documents.

The global soccer chief is alleged to have turned to politically-connected contacts to secure a new work permit for Yajarlin del Socorro Fernandez after the White House revoked her legal permission to work in the United States, according to documents reviewed by the Daily Mail.

The Nicaraguan-born Fernandez was reportedly employed by the soccer governing body to work as a housekeeper for the FIFA boss and his family in August 2024. Despite being on FIFA's payroll, she performed no services for the organization.

However, she reportedly continued illegally working in her role and living in the Infantino household for months after the Trump administration terminated the immigration agreement that granted her permission to stay in the United States.

Fernandez is then said to have secured a new work authorization under Kristi Noem's Department of Homeland Security following an intervention by a Trump adviser, documents show.

Infantino allegedly tapped Carlos Cordeiro, the former US Soccer chief who served as a senior World Cup adviser to Donald Trump, to orchestrate the new work permit.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino (right) reportedly enlisted the help of a Trump adviser to secure a work permit for his family's Nicaraguan housekeeper

Infantino allegedly tapped Carlos Cordeiro (pictured) to orchestrate a new work permit for Yajarlin del Socorro Fernandez

In January, Infantino reportedly asked Cordeiro, who in May 2025 was appointed to the White House's World Cup task force alongside Noem, to use his connections at the state department to smooth the path to getting Fernandez's new work visa approved, according to the documents.

Cordeiro also allegedly first helped to secure Fernandez's right to work in the US under Infantino's orders in 2024.

Fernandez was reportedly already living and working at Infantino's residence in Miami, Florida, in early 2024.

However, until May 2024, she had not yet filed or received an approved work permit and was therefore working at the residence illegally, per the documents.

During a January 2024 meeting at Infantino's home, Cordeiro, at the FIFA boss's request, is said to have instructed a subordinate to submit their own Miami rental address on Fernandez's immigration filing rather than that of the Infantino family home.

While Fernandez's work visa was initially approved, it came to an abrupt end last year when the Department of Homeland Security terminated the Humanitarian Parole Program for Cuba, Haiti, Venezuela and her native Nicaragua.

On May 30, 2025, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to scrap the four-country scheme, which had permitted Fernandez and other Nicaraguans to secure permission to work in the US.

Fernandez's contract with FIFA was terminated in October 2025, but she was paid a three-month salary as a bonus and remained illegally working as Infantino's housekeeper for the remainder of the year, according to the documents.

Cordeiro (left) was appointed to Trump's White House's World Cup task force in 2025

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem worked in connection with the task force

In January 2026, Infantino allegedly asked Cordeiro, who was now working on the World Cup task force which operated directly out of Homeland Security, to leverage his new government contacts to secure Fernandez a new permit. That same month, Fernandez was granted a new work visa.

There is no suggestion that Fernandez personally is accused of any wrongdoing.

FIFA strongly denied the allegations that it had 'employed an individual in the US without the necessary authorisation.'

'FIFA verifies the employment status of each employee and ensures compliance with U.S. immigration and employment requirements,' a FIFA spokesperson told The Daily Mail.

'Matters related to the FIFA President's personal and home life are private; however, for the avoidance of any doubt, the costs of any domestic staff are met by the FIFA President personally.

The organization added: 'As FIFA stated in August, it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President. FIFA welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a license to amplify false allegations. Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading FIFA will continue to challenge it directly and vigorously.'

Cordeiro did not immediately respond to The Daily Mail's requests for comment. However, he declined to address his alleged role to The New York Post, claiming he was 'not aware of the story.'

In a statement to the Daily Mail, a spokesperson for the DHS said: 'On December 16, 2023, Yajarlin del Socor Fernandez, an alien from Nicaragua, was permitted entry into the United States through the now-defunct Biden-era CHNV parole program.

'Del Socor Fernandez re-applied for lawful status in December 2025 and was approved to remain in the United States until January 2027.'

Infantino, who is standing for reelection in 2027, has faced months of scrutiny

The bombshell report comes after months of scrutiny for Infantino, who faces reelection in 2027.

Infantino faced mutiny earlier this year over his secret plans – later scrapped – to sell a stake in the World Cup to private equity investors including Joshua Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

It sparked uncertainty around Infantino's future after three confederations rejected his plan, which was then abandoned.

Among them was UEFA, which said it has lost confidence in Infantino and threatened to boycott future World Cups.

Cordeiro also recently quit FIFA over Infantino's commercial deals with Josh Kushner's Thrive Capital.

Infantino faced further scrutiny last month when it was alleged that Infantino personally intervened to suspend USA Folarin Balogun's World Cup red card following a call with President Trump.

In a saga that sparked condemnation from across the world, the striker was originally barred from the USA's last-16 match against Belgium, only for his ban to be sensationally suspended by the FIFA disciplinary committee following a protest by the White House. The New York Post claimed in October that Infantino told Trump in a call on July 1 that 'he would take care of it. One call and it was done.'

FIFA did not comment on the claims at the time but pointed to a July statement from Infantino, when he insisted the decision was made by 'independent' bodies acting 'autonomously.'

Despite mounting pressure over recent months, Infantino intends to stand for a fourth consecutive term next March at the FIFA Congress.

#1419. Marco Rose's Bournemouth should not have the depth to win this many games domestically and abroad but at Ipswich they showed they can do it the hard way, writes JAMES SHARPE

Published: 11:20 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 12:48 EST, 8 November 2026

Juggling domestic duties with European adventures should not be as manageable as this for teams like Bournemouth.

Clubs of their size should be creaking under the weight of the extra fixtures. All those games, all that travelling. They have played nine games in a month.

Far bigger outfits have toiled spinning those plates. Remember when Ange Postecoglou stopped bothering about the Premier League entirely just to focus on the Europa League.

And yet here are those brilliant Cherries, three days after a win in Prague in that same competition, making it eight on the bounce with a victory at Ipswich thanks to Evanilson's opener, following goalkeeper Christian Walton's early howler, and an own goal from Leif Davis.

Bournemouth haven't done that since 2013 when they were getting out of League One.

Now, they are seventh in the Premier League, second in the Europa League.

Leif Davies reacts after scoring an own goal to make it 2-0 to Bournemouth

And they're in the League Cup quarter-finals – all while having the squad depth to name Alex Scott and Junior Kroupi on the bench.

Marco Rose's side showed they can also do it the hard way, too, after Jack Clarke's second-half penalty for Ipswich, given for a soft foul on Abdoul Ouattara, provided a far more tense final 15 minutes than anticipated inside a feverish Portman Road where Julio Enciso also twice went close from late free-kicks.

'One goal changed the momentum of the game and that's why I'm much more pleased about the last 20 minutes because we suffered but we did it together,' said Rose.

First James Trafford, now Walton. Bournemouth's win over Leeds last weekend also hinged on a goalkeeping howler, when Trafford's simple pass out from the back was intercepted.

This time Ipswich stalwart Walton took a back pass from Dara O'Shea and decided the best course of action was to try to dummy and turn Evanilson. He failed, of course.

Evanilson rolled the ball into an empty net. That intense Bournemouth press really can do some crazy things to you.

IPSWICH (4-2-3-1): Walton 4; Ouattara 5, Diop 6, O'Shea 6, Davis 5; Florentino 7 (Akpom 85), Palacios 6; Maeda 6 (Fatawu 65, 7), Enciso 7; Philogene 6 (Clarke 54, 7); Emersonn 5 (Flemming 54, 6)

BOURNEMOUTH (4-2-3-1): Petrovic 6; Smith 6 (Diakite 79), Hill 7, Silva 7; Truffert 7; Adams 7, Christie 6 (Cook 67, 5); Rayan 6 (Adli 86), Kluivert 6 (Kroupi 68, 6), Tavernier 7; EVANILSON 8 (Rodriguez 85)

After scoring the opener in Bournemouth's win last weekend, manager Marco Rose told Evanilson that he was becoming a 'real No9'.

That's six goals now in his last seven games but it's his all-round play that's so impressive.

He dropped in and played a beautiful curling through ball into the channel to set Justin Kluivert free down the right.

He collected the loose ball for the second goal.

He made a fine run to latch on to a free-kick over the defence to stab the ball over to James Hill at the back post, who headed over from close range, which would have put him level with Declan Rice as the leading assister in the league too.

'He's so hard-working,' added Rose. 'He does everything out of possession.

'He starts the press, he plays in between the lines, he gives us deep runs.

'But the most important thing is scoring and he understood that he also needs to arrive close to goal if he wants to score.'

If the Tractor Boys are to make their stay in the Premier League a longer one than last time, they cannot afford to keep giving early leads. The mountain is steep enough.

Evanilson's opener was the sixth time Ipswich have conceded inside the first 15 minutes of a league game this season. They are yet to score one that early.

A howler from Ipswich keeper Christian Walton gifted Evanilson the opener

James Hill celebrates Bournemouth's win which lifts them to seventh

It is what will make this defeat especially frustrating for Gary O'Neil against his former club. 'Gary, what's the score?' chimed the travelling fans.

For so much of the contest, Ipswich looked composed and confident on the ball, played with energy and intent and, after they pulled one back, showed how much pressure they can put teams under and how much this place can bounce.

They are a much better side than the one that came up last time but you cannot come out after the break and have Ouattara give the ball straight to Evanilson again inside 30 seconds as he did before Ryan Christie's shot took two deflections and went in.

'Gutted,' said O'Neil. 'To lose a game that you haven't been outclassed is tough to take. We restricted Bournemouth to nothing of their own doing. If you give the ball to the opposition number nine twice, it's going to be difficult.'

#1418. Newcastle jeers tell Matthias Jaissle his ‘vertical’ football is not working

Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

Johan Manzambi heads Aston Villa in front! 🟣 https://t.co/jxZf2568Sl

It is getting hard to comprehend what Jaissle wants his team to do. The much-hyped “vertical” style looks like an ugly incarnation of the long ball football of yesteryear. They did not like it at Newcastle in the 1980s and 1990s and some fashions should never return. It is in danger of resembling a shell suit that has emerged from the back of the wardrobe for a Saturday night out.

There is so much confidence in the German in the Newcastle boardroom that they believe improvement is inevitable, but that is far from assured. Newcastle are not getting better; they are making all the same mistakes and, if anything, as an attacking force, they are looking increasingly stale and predictable. They did not have a shot on target in the first half and, other than one fantastic save in the second, Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki had nothing to do.

"If he doesn't slip Harvey Barnes in, he's got to hit the target" Shay Given discusses Newcastle's decision-making in the final third 🔲 https://t.co/wh4kCAEbxV

“Our decision-making in the final third was lacking today,” Jaissle said. “I am frustrated, I understand the supporters’ reaction, that is their right [to boo after a defeat at home].”

It is time for a sharp dose of medicine on Tyneside. Expectations need to be adjusted, especially as none of the new signings have impressed. This was always the fear and the risk when you put all your faith in young players from abroad.

For Jaissle’s vertical football to work, Newcastle need to be able to win the ball high up the pitch, whether that is with a high press or competing for second balls from long passes. They do not do either well. More worryingly, they look so vulnerable, so easy to play through.

Villa did it to them all afternoon. Nicolas Jackson should have scored in the first half, Ibrahim Mbaye should have hit the target in the second.

On another day, Newcastle could also have had centre-back Sven Botman sent off for a lunge on Jackson. Then it really would have become ugly, but the Dutchman survived a VAR check.

Villa were always the better side. There was no fluency in Newcastle’s game, no structure, no patterns of play. Every time they turned over the ball, they looked stretched. Every time they got a set-piece, it was defended easily. Every time they went forward in the first half, the ball was sent aimlessly long and came straight back at them. In the second, they huffed and puffed but did not sustain any pressure on the Villa goal. The missed chances late on were not clear opportunities and they were snatched at by the hapless Yoane Wissa.

Yoane Wissa fails to hit the target after an inspiring run! ❌ https://t.co/ohabzLZBRv

It was largely poor and so was the manner in which Villa took the lead. João Gomes was given the time and space to loft a cross to the far post for Manzambi, who had drifted away from Lewis Miley, to head home.

Newcastle were in disarray and it should have been 2-0 almost immediately when Emiliano Buendía received the ball in the middle of the area and crashed a shot against a post.

The home crowd tried to remain patient and supportive, but the sight of yet another long, aimless ball being punted forward straight to a Villa defender tipped some over the edge. There were boos and jeers in the stands while Jaissle screamed at Joe Willock and Wissa. There were more boos at half-time; things felt combustible.

Newcastle needed a big second half. They were better, but it was hardly anything to get excited about. A shot on the turn from Botman, superbly saved by Suzuki. Then a few half-chances were squandered, the occasional flash of a threat and that was it.

The Switzerland international’s decision to reject Newcastle in order to sign for Villa helped convince Eddie Howe to quit in the summer.
